The opponent has no unmortgaged properties with buildings. They cannot mortgage anything to raise cash. Their only remaining options are selling houses or hotels. I am now calculating exactly what they could liquidate.

Selling the opponent's red houses would raise about six hundred dollars. Their light blue houses are worth roughly two hundred dollars. The Connecticut hotel sale value is uncertain because hotel sales typically return four houses plus half the purchase price, and replacement rules vary.

The opponent cannot sell their hotels because the bank has no houses to replace them. They can only liquidate houses on properties that still have houses. Their red houses alone would raise about six hundred dollars.

Selling the opponent's light blue houses would raise about two hundred dollars. Selling their dark blue houses would add roughly four hundred dollars. The even-building rule may prevent selling Boardwalk hotel while Park Place still has houses.

The opponent is completely locked from selling any hotels. The bank has no houses to replace them. They cannot sell their dark blue hotel or their light blue hotel either. The even-building rule also prevents selling houses on the light blues while the Connecticut hotel remains.

All other properties are already mortgaged. They would go bankrupt.

Hotel construction on all three pinks would cost $300 and leave me with $1666. Any pink hit would then bankrupt the opponent completely, since their maximum liquidation is only about $694. I am now weighing this risk against the possibility that they might land on my properties instead.

I checked the standard Monopoly rent chart. Park Place with four houses costs $1300, and Boardwalk with a hotel costs $2000.

Rolling six from Pacific lands on Park Place for $1300, and rolling eight lands on Boardwalk for $2000. The opponent could also hit Chance and land on Boardwalk or other bad spaces.

After building hotels, I would have $1666. That covers Park Place but not Boardwalk. Selling a hotel returns half its purchase price plus four replacement houses.

Selling a hotel returns half its purchase price and four replacement houses. Those houses can then be sold for half price. This creates a two-step liquidation path if I build hotels.

Fully liquidating the three hotels would recover about seven hundred fifty dollars. The twelve replacement houses could then be sold for six hundred dollars. The net cost is essentially zero.

The opponent cannot build on Kentucky because one house costs $150 and they only have $94. Their light blue and dark blue sets are already maxed. I have $1966 and four properties with 4 houses each. The opponent has $94 and is heavily mortgaged. They are threatening light blues and reds. I am considering building or trading.

The opponent mortgaged Ventnor, Reading, and B&O to pay the $625 rent. Full liquidation would yield about $2786, covering both Park Place and Boardwalk hotels. I am now considering building hotels on the pink properties.

Building hotels on the three pinks costs $300. Each would raise rent by roughly $125 to $200, for a total gain of about $450. The opponent is currently on States Avenue and will roll from there next.

Hotel construction would return twelve houses to the bank. The opponent cannot build more houses with only ninety-four dollars. They might sell their hotels for half the purchase price to recover cash.

Selling a hotel returns half the purchase price. The opponent could sell Boardwalk or Connecticut to recover cash, but building on reds costs $150 per house. With only ninety-four dollars, they cannot afford to build much. Most of their properties are already mortgaged.

The opponent has no unmortgaged properties with buildings. They cannot mortgage anything to raise cash. Their only remaining options are selling houses or hotels. I am now calculating exactly what they could liquidate.

Selling the opponent's red houses would raise about six hundred dollars. Their light blue houses are worth roughly two hundred dollars. The Connecticut hotel sale value is uncertain because hotel sales typically return four houses plus half the purchase price, and replacement rules vary.

The opponent cannot sell their hotels because the bank has no houses to replace them. They can only liquidate houses on properties that still have houses. Their red houses alone would raise about six hundred dollars.

Selling the opponent's light blue houses would raise about two hundred dollars. Selling their dark blue houses would add roughly four hundred dollars. The even-building rule may prevent selling Boardwalk hotel while Park Place still has houses.

The opponent is completely locked from selling any hotels. The bank has no houses to replace them. They cannot sell their dark blue hotel or their light blue hotel either. The even-building rule also prevents selling houses on the light blues while the Connecticut hotel remains.

The opponent can sell red houses because the difference between two and three is only one level. They cannot sell light blue houses until they sell the Connecticut hotel, which they cannot do without bank houses. Dark blue properties are also locked because selling the Boardwalk hotel requires four replacement houses.

The opponent can raise about six hundred ninety-four dollars by selling their red houses and keeping ninety-four dollars. They can pay the six hundred twenty-five dollar rent on St. Charles or States Avenue with that cash. They cannot pay the seven hundred dollar rent on Virginia Avenue. All other properties are already mortgaged. They would go bankrupt.

Hotel construction on all three pinks would cost $300 and leave me with $1666. Any pink hit would then bankrupt the opponent completely, since their maximum liquidation is only about $694. I am now weighing this risk against the possibility that they might land on my properties instead.

I checked the standard Monopoly rent chart. Park Place with four houses costs $1300, and Boardwalk with a hotel costs $2000.

Rolling six from Pacific lands on Park Place for $1300, and rolling eight lands on Boardwalk for $2000. The opponent could also hit Chance and land on Boardwalk or other bad spaces.

After building hotels, I would have $1666. That covers Park Place but not Boardwalk. Selling a hotel returns half its purchase price plus four replacement houses.

Selling a hotel returns half its purchase price and four replacement houses. Those houses can then be sold for half price. This creates a two-step liquidation path if I build hotels.

Fully liquidating the three hotels would recover about seven hundred fifty dollars. The twelve replacement houses could then be sold for six hundred dollars. The net cost is essentially zero.

Fully liquidating the three hotels would return about $750, which is $150 more than selling the twelve houses directly. The net gain from hoteling is roughly $150.

Hoteling reduces maximum liquidation by about $150. Full liquidation after building hotels would reach roughly $2636, which still covers both Boardwalk and Park Place. I can survive both dark blue properties even after hoteling.

I am now weighing whether the win chance from hoteling is worth the risk of losing those hotels before bankruptcy. I also need to verify the turn order, since the opponent just paid rent on States Avenue and it is my post-turn decision.

Turn 180 is my turn. I landed on Pacific Avenue and will end it. The opponent will then roll from States Avenue.

I am mapping the exact board order to verify the opponent's roll destinations from States Avenue. The sequence runs through Virginia Avenue, Pennsylvania Railroad, St. James Place, Community Chest, Tennessee Avenue, New York Avenue, Free Parking, Kentucky Avenue, Chance, Indiana Avenue, Illinois Avenue, B&O Railroad, Atlantic Avenue, Ventnor Avenue, Water Works, Marvin Gardens, Go to Jail, Pacific Avenue, North Carolina Avenue, Community Chest, Pennsylvania Avenue, Short Line Railroad, Chance, Park Place, Luxury Tax, Boardwalk, and GO.

The opponent's roll destinations from States Avenue are now mapped. A roll of one is impossible with two dice, so the minimum is two. Only rolls two and five land on my properties, both mortgaged at zero rent. The other outcomes are mostly theirs or neutral spaces.

The opponent cannot land on my pink properties from States Avenue next turn. The closest pink behind them is Virginia, which is only one space away, so that roll is impossible. They would need to go all the way around the board to reach any of my pinks.

The opponent would need to roll a forty from States Avenue to reach St. Charles Place, which is thirty-eight spaces away. That is impossible with two dice.

Rolling six from Pacific lands on Park Place for $1300 and rolling eight lands on Boardwalk for $2000. Both are high-risk outcomes. I am now weighing whether to build hotels before my next roll, since I can survive both dark blues through liquidation alone.

Without hotels, selling one house for fifty dollars would still leave me with sixteen dollars and eleven houses, so the pink properties remain dangerous. Building hotels now would give the opponent replacement houses during their turn while I am weaker. The opponent currently has ninety-four dollars and owns red properties at two and three houses each.

The opponent cannot build on Kentucky because one house costs $150 and they only have $94. Their light blue and dark blue sets are already maxed. They lack a complete orange set since Tennessee is mortgaged by me. The green properties are all mortgaged, so building would require paying unmortgage fees totaling about $143.

The opponent cannot unmortgage the green properties. Ventnor and Marvin Gardens together require about four hundred forty dollars to fully restore, but the opponent only has ninety-four dollars. Selling red houses to raise cash would be a poor investment, since they would need to rebuild elsewhere and lose the houses entirely. They might sell red houses for a small cash cushion against future pink hits, though that is still not a sound move.

Returning the twelve replacement houses would let the opponent sell the Boardwalk hotel and its four replacement houses for about five hundred dollars. They could also sell the Park Place houses for four hundred dollars, plus their red houses for six hundred dollars, giving them roughly nine hundred dollars in cash. That would allow them to pay the rent on my pink properties.

If I return the twelve replacement houses, the opponent could liquidate all buildings for roughly $1919. That would let them survive both dark blue rents and potentially rebuild. Without returning the houses, they can only raise about $694 from red houses alone, which is insufficient to pay the $700 rent on Virginia Avenue or the $625 rent on St. Charles Place. Their hotels would also remain frozen, since they cannot sell a hotel without houses in the bank.

I will not build hotels. The opponent cannot sell their frozen hotels to raise cash, so the house shortage itself is the most dangerous weapon. Hoteling would cost three hundred dollars and reduce my Boardwalk survival margin. It would also release twelve houses that could let them liquidate dark blues and light blues to survive my rent. I should keep the current four-house pinks as they are.

I can survive both dark blue properties without hotels. Paying Park Place from cash leaves me with six hundred sixty-six dollars and eleven houses. Paying Boardwalk requires selling one house for fifty dollars, leaving me with sixteen dollars and eleven houses. I still cannot afford the Virginia Avenue rent of seven hundred dollars. I am also weighing possible negative chance cards.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad or Tennessee Avenue is not worthwhile. The railroad would only yield twenty-five dollars in rent while the other two are mortgaged, and Tennessee does not complete an orange set. I am now considering a trade with the opponent to accelerate their bankruptcy.

I am now weighing whether to propose a trade. The opponent would not sell their pink properties or give me cash, so a deal would not help them bankrupt. I will likely keep the current strategy and wait for the housing shortage to force them into bankruptcy.

I considered trading Tennessee Avenue to complete the opponent's orange set, but that would give them a mortgaged monopoly they cannot unmortgage. I will not offer it.

I will keep my Get Out of Jail Free cards. If I land in jail, the board path from there to my pink properties passes through my own spaces and far away from their dark blues. I have two such cards.

I will end my turn. I will not build, sell, unmortgage, or trade.

The opponent has no Get Out of Jail Free cards. They will likely propose a trade on their turn to raise cash.
